blocks.text: As the histopathology shows carbon-laden macrophages, it is not associated with Psittacosis which is a zoonotic bacterial infection caused by Chlamydia psittaci, contracted from exposure to infected birds, such as parrots. blocks.title: Coal Worker’s Pneumoconiosis (CWP)
rows: It is characterised by coal macules (1 to 2 mm in diameter) and larger coal nodules containing carbon-laden macrophages and a delicate network of collagen fibres. Although these lesions are scattered throughout the lung, the upper lobes and upper zones of the lower lobes are more heavily involved. Dilatation of alveoli adjacent to bronchioles gives rise to centrilobular emphysema.

It leads to progressive massive fibrosis and large, dark scars measuring 1 to 10 cm in diameter, often appearing in multiple areas. Microscopically, these lesions contain dense collagen and pigment deposition. Lung function is compromised

blocks.text: The chest X-ray shows calcification of hilar lymph nodes, called eggshell calcification. The clinical picture, along with eggshell calcification, suggests silicosis.
**Silicosis:** It is the most prevalent occupational lung disease in the world.
**Cause:** Inhalation of proinflammatory crystalline silicon dioxide (silica). After decades of exposure, it usually presents as slowly progressing, nodular, fibrosing pneumoconiosis.
**Occupations at risk:**

**Pathogenesis:** Phagocytosis of inhaled silica crystals by macrophages activates the inflammasome and stimulates the release of inflammatory mediators, particularly IL-1 and IL-18. This, in turn, recruits additional inflammatory cells and activates interstitial fibroblasts, leading to collagen deposition.
**Forms of silica:** Amorphous.
**Crystalline (quartz, cristobalite, and tridymite)**- more fibrogenic.
**Forms of silicosis:**

items.text: **Acute:** Heavy exposure in closed spaces Associated with Silico-tuberculosis and Secondary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis ( SPAP) Can present within 2 years.
**Chronic Complicated:** Chronic cough and progressive dyspnea on exertion.
**Morphology:** Discrete nodules in hilar nodes and upper zones of lungs.
Fibrotic lesions in nodes and pleura (pleural thickening).
Eggshell calcification (thin sheets of calcification in lymph nodes; calcium surrounding a zone lacking calcification).

blocks.text: **Histological hallmark:** Central collagen with a peripheral zone of dust-laden macrophages.

items.text: **CT scan:** Crazy pavement pattern and interstitial fibrosis.
**Byssinosis (Option A):** Caused by inhalation of cotton dust, common in textile workers. Presents with Monday chest tightness — not associated with eggshell calcification.
**Asbestosis (Option C):** Exposure to asbestos leads to lower lobe fibrosis, pleural plaques, and increased risk of mesothelioma — but eggshell calcification is not typical.
**Berylliosis (Option D):** Occurs in aerospace, electronics, and nuclear industries. Presents with non-caseating granulomas, similar to sarcoidosis. Eggshell calcification is not characteristic.

blocks.text: Eggshell calcification is not seen in metastatic lymph nodes. Eggshell calcification refers to a ring of calcification at the periphery of a lymph node (thin sheets of calcification in lymph nodes; calcium surrounding a zone lacking calcification).
**Causes:**

Amphibole (crocidolite, amosite) is the most toxic form of asbestos. Asbestos is a family of crystalline hydrated silicates associated with pulmonary fibrosis and various forms of cancer. It occurs in two distinct geometric forms: serpentine and amphibole. Amphiboles are straight and stiffly aligned with the airstream and can be delivered deeper into the lungs. They can penetrate epithelial cells and reach the interstitium.

Chrysolites, with their more flexible, curled structure, are likely to become impacted in the upper respiratory passages and removed by the mucociliary elevator. Even if they get trapped in the lungs, they are easily removed as they are more soluble. Both amphiboles and serpentines are fibrogenic and are associated with a higher incidence of asbestos-related diseases.

rows: More pathogenic (amphiboles particularly associated with mesothelioma )

**Byssinosis:** Cotton dust/ organic dust exposure. The patient usually complains that the symptoms worsen when they come to work on Monday, hence the name Monday disease. They get better when off work, and symptoms reduce as the week progresses. This cycle is repeated.

**Bagassosis** is caused by inhaling the fibrous cane-sugar residue called bagasse. It occurs in those working with bagasse, such as those in wallboard or paper manufacturing, but is not seen in sugar industry workers.
**Siderosis** is due to exposure to iron oxide in welders.
**Berylliosis** is caused by beryllium exposure. It leads to non-caseating granulomas, as in sarcoidosis and can be differentiated based on industry exposure.
**Mesothelioma:** A rare cancer arising from mesothelial cells that most commonly affects the pleura. It can also affect the peritoneum, pericardium and tunica vaginalis.
**Aetiology:**
**Asbestos:** Mesothelioma is the most specific asbestos-associated cancer (Option A). It is not associated with smoking (Option D).
**Pathology:** Advanced pleural mesothelioma can cause extensive pleural fibrosis and thickening, making the affected side rigid and immobile.
Later stages fix the mediastinum in place due to pleural thickening and fibrosis. The mediastinal shift is not a characteristic feature of mesothelioma.
**M/C cytogenetic abnormality in mesothelioma:** Homozygous deletion of chromosome 9p, leading to loss of tumour suppressor gene- CDKN2A.
**Clinical features:**

items.text: Progressive dyspnea, chest pain, weight loss, chronic cough, hemoptysis.
Decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion (due to pleural effusion or thickening).

blocks.text: **Diagnosis:**

items.text: **CT scan:** Pleural thickening, effusion, or frozen hemithorax (not causing a mediastinal shift in the presence of effusion) (Options C and D)

**Confirmed by biopsy:** Epithelioid mesothelioma shows tubules, nests, or papillary structures with uniform round to oval nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm. Sarcomatoid mesothelioma consists of spindle-shaped cells resembling fibrosarcoma. Biphasic mesothelioma displays a mixture of both patterns.

items.text: **Option B. Silicosis:** Silicosis is a lung disease caused by the inhalation of crystalline silica dust. It leads to the development of fibrous tissue in the lungs, similar to asbestosis. However, silicosis is characterized by the presence of silica particles within the lung tissue rather than asbestos bodies. Occupational exposure to industries such as mining, sandblasting, or stone cutting is commonly associated with silicosis.

**Option C. Tuberculosis:** Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs but can also involve other organs. TB is characterized by the formation of granulomas, which are nodular inflammatory lesions, in the affected tissues. In the lungs, TB granulomas typically contain caseous necrosis, which appears as cheesy or crumbly material on histopathology. While TB can cause lung fibrosis in advanced cases, the thickening of the pleura mentioned in the question is not a typical finding of tuberculosis.

**Option D. Mesothelioma:** Mesothelioma is a type of cancer that affects the mesothelium, the thin membrane that lines the chest cavity and covers the lungs. It is primarily caused by exposure to asbestos fibers. Histopathologically, mesothelioma is characterized by malignant cells forming a disorganized pattern within the mesothelium. While mesothelioma can cause lung fibrosis in some cases, thickening of the pleura is a more prominent feature associated with asbestosis rather than mesothelioma.

blocks.text: The clinical presentation and the gross specimen showing emphysematous damage involving the enlargement of the entire acinus are consistent with panacinar emphysema. This pattern of emphysema is most commonly associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
**Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency:** It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the alpha-1 antitrypsin gene located on Chromosome 14.

Normal individuals have the PiMM genotype, while those with the disease have the PiZZ genotype. This results in significantly reduced levels of functional alpha-1 antitrypsin protein. Carriers possess the PiMZ genotype. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to panacinar emphysema and the liver, causing cirrhosis due to abnormal protein accumulation.
Emphysema is classified according to its anatomic distribution within the lobule.
Based on the segments of the respiratory units that are involved, emphysema is subdivided into four major types:

The most common lung finding in COVID-19 infections is diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), characterized by injury to the alveolar epithelium and endothelium, leading to pulmonary oedema, inflammation and the formation of hyaline membranes.
**COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2):**
**Transmission:** It likely originated from a seafood and animal market in Wuhan. Initial animal-to-human transmission, followed by human-to-human spread.

**Clinical features:** Range from mild flu-like symptoms to severe respiratory illness. Severe cases often involve respiratory compromise and bilateral ground-glass opacities on chest imaging. It is more severe in older adults and individuals with comorbidities (e.g., diabetes, COPD, heart failure).
**Pathology:** Histologic analysis of lung tissue shows diffuse alveolar damage and inflammation, primarily with mononuclear cells.

The given scenario of cough, fever, hemoptysis, and a cavitary lesion with caseous necrosis at the right lung apex strongly suggests Pulmonary Tuberculosis, which involves a type-4 hypersensitivity reaction. CD4+ T cells activate macrophages, but Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives within them, causing granuloma formation with caseous necrosis, driven by a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction and resulting in tissue damage.
It is a bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and can be classified into the following types:
**1. Primary tuberculosis** It develops in a previously unexposed and, therefore, unsensitized person. The primary organ involved is mostly the lungs.
**Location:** Sub-pleural region. Lower part of the upper lobe & upper part of the lower lobe.
**Ghon’s focus:** Grey-white area of inflammation with consolidation.
**Ghon’s complex:** Ghon’s focus + inflamed regional lymph nodes.
**Histology:** Granulomatous inflammatory reaction with both caseating and non-caseating tubercles.
**Simon’s focus:** Occult hematogenous dissemination to the apex of the lung.

**Fate:** 95% of the cases are controlled by immunity, calcified, healed lesions and hilar lymph nodes (Ranke complex). 5% of the cases are progressive (Progressive primary TB). Resembles acute bacterial pneumonia.
Lymphohematogenous dissemination may cause tuberculous meningitis and/or miliary TB.

**2. Secondary tuberculosis** It arises in a previously sensitised host. It may follow shortly after primary tuberculosis, but more commonly, it appears months to years after the initial infection, usually when the host resistance is weakened. The apical and posterior lobe segments are involved due to high O 2 concentration (Puhl’s focus).
The infraclavicular lesion is called Assman’s focus. Regional lymph node involvement is late. Cavitation occurs readily with the erosion of the cavities into an airway.
**Histology:** Active lesions show coalescent tubercles with central caseation (Caseous necrosis).
**3. Disseminated TB:** Spread to other organs.

The images below show the caseous necrosis seen in TB. Enzyme degradation (Option A) may be involved in the breakdown of tissue during infection. The primary mechanism of tissue damage in tuberculosis is the type-4 hypersensitivity reaction.

items.text: **Fibrinoid deposition (Option C):** refers to the accumulation of fibrin-like material in the walls of blood vessels. It is typically associated with conditions such as vasculitis.

**Sudden cutoff of blood supply (Option D):** occurs when the blood supply to a tissue is abruptly interrupted, leading to ischemia and subsequent tissue death. In the case of tuberculosis, the tissue damage is primarily caused by the immune response and the formation of granulomas.

blocks.text: The histopathological image shows ferruginous bodies, suggestive of Asbestosis, indicating the person likely worked in the asbestos industry. It is a chronic lung condition caused by the inhalation of asbestos fibres over a prolonged period. These fibres accumulate in the lung tissue, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and scarring.
**Symptoms:** Includes shortness of breath, coughing, and chest tightness
**The histopathological features seen in asbestosis include:**

**Interstitial fibrosis:** Asbestos fibres cause injury to the lung parenchyma, resulting in the deposition of collagen and fibrous tissue in the interstitium. This fibrosis leads to thickening of the alveolar walls and restrictive lung function.

**Ferruginous bodies:** Asbestos fibres can be recognized in the lung tissue as long, golden-brown, rod-shaped structures called ferruginous bodies. These bodies are composed of asbestos fibre coated with iron and protein.

items.text: **Silica (Option A):** exposure is associated with a lung disease called silicosis. Histopathological features of silicosis include nodular lesions with silica particles, collagenous fibrosis, and concentric silicotic nodules featuring central collagen and a peripheral zone of dust-laden macrophages.

**Coal dust (Option C):** exposure is associated with coal worker's pneumoconiosis (CWP). Histopathological features of CWP include the presence of coal macules (collections of carbon-laden macrophages) and coal nodules (fibrotic lesions with central cores of coal dust).

**Cotton (Option D):** exposure can lead to a lung disease known as byssinosis, also called brown lung disease. Histopathological findings in byssinosis include bronchiolitis and chronic bronchitis with peribronchiolar fibrosis.

blocks.text: In the electron microscopic image of the lung tissue, the structure labelled "A" represents the endothelium, where SARS-CoV-2 infection would impact and cause expansion. It is the virus causing COVID-19. It leads to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

**Mechanism:** The virus can directly infect the endothelial cells that line the blood vessels in the lungs, disrupting the normal function and integrity of the endothelial cells, resulting in increased vascular permeability, inflammation, and the onset of pulmonary edema. (Option B)

**Layer B (Option A)** represents the basal lamina, which offers structural support to the epithelial cells and separates them from the underlying connective tissue. However, it is not the primary site of infection in SARS-CoV-2-related ARDS.

**Layer D (Option C)** represents epithelium that lines the airways and plays a key role in the respiratory system's defence mechanisms. However, it is not the primary target in SARS-CoV-2-related ARDS, where the main pathological changes occur in the endothelium.

blocks.text: Asbestosis, a pneumoconiosis caused by asbestos inhalation, is strongly associated with mesothelioma, a malignancy of the pleura or peritoneum. Asbestos exposure also increases the risk of lung, laryngeal, ovarian, colon, and pleural cancers. Smoking significantly amplifies the risk of asbestos-related lung carcinoma, making asbestos workers, especially smokers, more likely to die from lung cancer than mesothelioma.

Compared to other occupational lung diseases, which affect the upper lobes of the lungs, it commonly affects the lower lobes. Adenocarcinoma (primary bronchogenic carcinoma ) is the most common type of cancer, accounting for about 45%, followed by squamous cell carcinoma. Lung mesothelioma is a more specific tumour associated with asbestos exposure. It is common but is less prevalent than Adenocarcinoma.

**Anthracosis (Option B):** , associated with bronchial arthrofibrosis (BAF), is a condition characterised by the black staining of the bronchial mucosa, which can obstruct the bronchial lumen. It typically manifests in elderly non-smokers, either male or female, with a chronic course of symptoms like dyspnea and/or cough. It occurs due to the accumulation of carbon, silica, and quartz particles in macrophages, mucosa, and submucosa, leading to anthracosis.

**Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (Option C):** is the most common form of primary liver cancer. It typically develops in individuals with chronic liver diseases such as cirrhosis, which can be caused by chronic Hepatitis B or C infection. Other causes of cirrhosis include alcohol abuse, autoimmune diseases, chronic liver inflammation, and iron overload (hemochromatosis). HCC arises from long-term liver damage and scarring.

**Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) (Option D):** is the most common type, accounting for approximately 90–95% of adult kidney cancers. It originates in the lining of the proximal convoluted tubules (PCTs). Symptoms of RCC include blood in the urine, flank pain, abdominal mass, weight loss, fever, high blood pressure, night sweats, and malaise. When RCC metastasises, it commonly spreads to the lymph nodes, lungs, liver, adrenal glands, brain, or bones.
